svg.title: Heat fluxes between the sea-ice, slab-ocean and three-dimensional ocean modules
svg.desc: Two columns, an ice-covered point (left) and an open-water point (right), drawn through five stacked layers that are not to scale: atmosphere, snow, sea ice, the 50 m slab mixed layer and the 16-layer three-dimensional ocean. Each arrow points in its flux’s positive direction. Left: the net atmospheric heat flux Q_a, positive downward, is the sum of net shortwave, net longwave, sensible and latent heat flux, averaged over the N atmosphere steps of one coupling window: Q_a = (1/N) Σ (SW + LW + SH + LH)_k. It reaches the snow/ice surface at temperature T_i. For ice at least h_min thick, the surface energy balance (C_i/Δt)(T_i^(n+1) − T_i^n) = Q_a − K_z(T_i^(n+1) − T_o^n) gives T_i^(n+1). If this gives T_i^(n+1) ≤ T_m, nothing melts and Q_m = 0. If it gives T_i^(n+1) > T_m, T_i^(n+1) is set to the melting point T_m instead and the surplus heat melts snow and ice: Q_m = Q_a − K_z(T_m − T_o^n) − (C_i/Δt)(T_m − T_i^n) > 0, the heat coming in minus the heat conducted to the slab minus the heat that warms the surface to T_m. On thin ice (0 < h_i < h_min), T_i^(n+1) = T_o^n and Q_m = Q_a. Q_m melts snow first, at the rate M_s = max[0, min(S/Δt, Q_m/(ρ_w L_s))], and the remainder Q_m^rem = Q_m − ρ_w L_s M_s, positive only after all snow melts, goes to the ice ledger, as does the snow-to-ice flux Q_s→i ≤ 0 of flooded snow at the snow base. Conduction through snow and ice runs from T_i to the slab temperature T_o and is split at the freezing point T_f at the ice base. The upper part, K_z(T_i^(n+1) − T_f), stays in the ledger Q_ice = K_z(T_i^(n+1) − T_f) + Q_o→i + Q_m^rem + Q_s→i, which updates h_i^(n+1) = h_i^n − Q_ice Δt/(ρ_i L_i); Q_ice > 0 melts and Q_ice < 0 grows ice, and thickness above h_max becomes Q_max, taken off Q_a at the next step. The lower part, Q_i→o = Q_f = K_z(T_f − T_o^n), goes down to the slab, plus the leftover melt energy if the ice melts away. Under ice the slab temperature does not take up these fluxes: the slab is reset to T_f and passes all its heat to the ice, Q_o→i = Q_i→o + Q_deep + (C_o/Δt)(T_o^n − T_f), that is, the heat from the ice, the heat from the 3-D ocean and the heat of resetting the slab from T_o^n to T_f; the ice uses it at the next step. Right: with no ice, T_i^(n+1) = T_o^n, Q_m = 0 and the sea-ice module only passes Q_i→o = Q_a − ρ_w L_s P_s to the slab, where ρ_w L_s P_s melts the snowfall P_s. The slab first takes up this step’s heat, giving the updated SST T_o* = T_o^n + (Δt/C_o)(Q_i→o + Q_deep). If T_o^n < T_f it resets T_o to T_f and returns Q_o→i = (C_o/Δt)(T_o* − T_f) < 0, which grows new ice at the next step; otherwise T_o^(n+1) = T_o* and Q_o→i = 0. Bottom: the top 50 m layer of the three-dimensional ocean, T^(0), is reset to T_o every step, and the deep-ocean flux Q_deep = ρ_0 c_p,0 (T^(0)_new − T_o) h_0/Δt, limited to ±2000 W m⁻² and zero in slab-only runs, enters the slab in both columns; advection, diffusion and convection link the columns. Under established ice the slab starts each step at T_o^n = T_f, so Q_i→o = Q_f = 0, the slab-reset term vanishes and Q_o→i = Q_deep.
